newsitem.title: USA: AT&T first-quarter income down, BellSouth up.
newsitem.headline: AT&T first-quarter income down, BellSouth up.

text.p: AT&T Corp. said Monday its first-quarter profits fell 17 percent, trimmed by competition in long-distance services and the cost of investments in new areas of business.

AT&T said it earned $1.13 billion, or 69 cents a share, on revenue of $13.05 billion, which compared with net income of $1.36 billion, or 85 cents a share, on revenue of $12.85 billion in the first quarter of 1996.

BellSouth Corp., meanwhile, said its earnings rose in the first quarter, due to an increase in the number of customer lines and strong growth in its wireless operations, both in the United States and overseas.
AT&T's income per share was in line with Wall Street's expectations as well as those of the company.
"Results are where we expected them to be as we implement our strategy," Chairman Robert E. Allen said in a statement.

The revenue increase was driven by growth in local telephone service and other initiatives, business long-distance services and wireless services. That was partially offset by declines in financial services and consumer long-distance revenues, the company said.
AT&T said long-distance calling volume in the most recent quarter increased by 6.7 percent over the same period of 1996, but revenue from those services rose only 0.6 percent to $11.51 billion.
Volume from consumer long-distance was flat and revenue fell 1 percent to $6.06 billion, the company said. Revenue from business long-distance rose 2.4 percent on a double-digit increase in volume.
AT&T said expansion in online, local and international operations reduced its quarterly per share income by 25 cents. A year earlier, those expenses reduced earnings by 10 cents a share, AT&T said.

In addition, ATT it increased hiring of customer support staff for marketing of new services and for wireless operations, boosting the total number of employees to 134,000, a net rise of 3,600 jobs during the first quarter of 1997.
The quickened pace of hiring more than offset reductions resulting from the company's ongoing, three-year restructuring plan announced January 2, 1996, the company said.
To date, 6,100 employees have left the company, primarily in backoffice, corporate support staff functions as part of the plan to reduce the workforce by 17,000 over three years.
Atlanta-based BellSouth said it earned $693 million, or 70 cents a share, on revenues of $4.8 billion in the three months ended March 31.

A year earlier the international communications services company earned $626 million, or 63 cents a share, before a one-time gain of $344 million, or 35 cents a share, on the sale of paging operations.
Revenues were $4.5 billion in the 1996 quarter.
"BellSouth's 17th consecutive quarter of improved operating results was driven by our innovative marketing," said Duane Ackerman, president and chief executive officer.
The company said the number of customer lines increased by 379,000 -- the biggest gain for any quarter in the company's history, breaking the old mark of 359,000 set in the first quarter of 1996.

It added that sales of calling features and convenience services, such as Caller ID, Caller ID Deluxe, Call Waiting and MemoryCall service voice messaging, continued to grow rapidly, posting a 24 percent increase.

BellSouth said the company's U.S. cellular operations ended the first quarter with 3.8 million customers, an annual growth rate of 24 percent. In international cellular markets, customers increased 76 percent since the first quarter of 1996, reaching 1.5 million.
BellSouth stock was down 37.5 cents at $40.625 and AT&T stock was down 75 cents at $33, both in morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
